items.q: The RabbitMQ model: exchange, queue, binding, routing key?
items.a:
The producer sends a message to an [[b:exchange]] → the exchange routes it into a [[b:queue]] via a [[b:binding]] + routing key.

**Exchange types:**
- direct (exact match)
- topic (wildcard)
- fanout (broadcast)
- headers

RabbitMQ is a [[g:'smart broker, dumb consumer']] — the broker owns routing and message state.

:::deep
- [[b:direct]]: routing key matches exactly (dispatch by type)
- [[b:topic]]: wildcard `*`/`#` (e.g. `booking.*.created`)
- [[b:fanout]]: broadcasts to every bound queue (pub/sub)
- [[b:headers]]: matches on headers

Durability: only *durable queue* + *persistent message* + *quorum queue* (Raft, replacing the old mirrored queue) survives a node loss.

OTA: a topic exchange routes `payment.succeeded`/`booking.cancelled` to several consumers (ticketing, notification, loyalty); a priority queue handles OTP/urgent transactions.

[[r:a long queue (backlog) means consumers can't keep up]] → scale consumers or raise prefetch.
:::

items.q: The Kafka model: topic, partition, offset, consumer group?
items.a:
Kafka is an immutable [[g:distributed log]]:
- a [[b:topic]] is split into [[b:partition]]s
- each message has a monotonically increasing [[b:offset]] within its partition
- consumers in the same [[b:consumer group]] split the partitions between them (one consumer per partition) → parallel scaling

[[g:'Dumb broker, smart consumer']] — the consumer manages its own offset. Messages are kept per retention (not deleted on read) → [[g:replayable]].

:::deep
- messages are kept per [[b:retention]] (time/size), NOT deleted on read → multiple consumer groups can read independently and replay (by resetting the offset)
- each partition is handled by one consumer within a group (useful consumer count ≤ partition count)
- committing the offset means 'processed up to here' → commit *after* processing (at-least-once), never auto-commit before processing

OTA: Kafka acts as the event backbone (booking CDC → search/loyalty/analytics, immutable audit, event-sourcing ledger); size partitions for throughput and consumer count ([[r:reducing partition count later is hard]] → over-provision moderately). Key = `booking_id` to preserve event order for a given booking.
:::

items.q: RabbitMQ vs Kafka — when do you use which?
items.a:
RabbitMQKafka
Modelsmart broker (queue)distributed log
After readingmessage disappears (ack)kept per retention → replay
Routingflexible (exchange)partitioned by key
Throughputhighextremely high (millions of msg/s)
Good fortask queues, RPC, command dispatchevent streams, sourcing, analytics
:::tip Bottom line RabbitMQ = a task queue with smart routing; Kafka = a durable distributed log with replay and high throughput. Many systems use both. ::: :::deep - [[g:RabbitMQ]] when you need flexible routing, task queues/RPC, low latency for discrete work, per-message TTL/priority, 'send a command to a consumer' - [[g:Kafka]] when you need massive throughput, storage & replay, multiple independent consumers, event sourcing/log pipelines/analytics, partition-scoped ordering [[r:Don't force one broker to do everything.]] OTAs typically use BOTH: Kafka as the event bus/CDC/analytics backbone, RabbitMQ for routed tasks (dispatching tickets through a provider, retry jobs). :::

items.q: What do the delivery semantics at-most-once / at-least-once / exactly-once mean?
items.a:
SemanticsLoss?Duplicates?Notes
At-most-oncepossiblenofire-and-forget
At-least-oncenopossibleretries until ack → consumer must be idempotent
Exactly-oncenonoideal; essentially unattainable end-to-end
In practice you achieve [[g:effectively-once]] = at-least-once + dedup/idempotency on the consumer side. :::deep - [[r:end-to-end exactly-once is essentially unattainable]] (the ack can be lost over the network after processing already happened) → effectively-once - Kafka offers 'exactly-once semantics' but only *within Kafka's own scope* (idempotent producer + read-process-write transactions across topics) — it doesn't extend to external side effects (PSP, external DB) - at-most-once is only for data that can afford to be lost (raw metrics) Fintech/OTA: every money/ticket flow = at-least-once + idempotency key + dedup table → 'processing may repeat, but the effect happens once'. [[r:Never trust 'exactly-once' for a side effect outside the system.]] :::

items.q: How do RabbitMQ Publisher Confirms and consumer ack/prefetch work?
items.a:
- [[b:Publisher Confirms]]: the broker acks back to the producer once it has received (and persisted) the message → the producer knows for certain the message reached the broker; async confirms (tracked by delivery tag) give high throughput
- [[b:Consumer ack]] (manual): the consumer only acks after finishing processing → dying mid-way triggers redelivery
- [[b:Prefetch (QoS)]]: caps the number of un-acked messages per consumer → stops one consumer hogging everything and balances load

:::tip Bottom line
confirms guarantee 'the broker received it'; manual ack guarantees 'it was processed'. Together they only give at-least-once → the consumer still has to be idempotent.
:::

:::deep
- proper async confirm: store unconfirmed messages in a `ConcurrentNavigableMap` keyed by *deliveryTag*; `basic.ack` (multiple=true → clears everything ≤ tag), `basic.nack` → retry/republish. [[r:Don't confirm each message synchronously]] (kills throughput)
- only confirms + persistent messages + durable queue + mirrored/quorum queue together guarantee nothing is lost on broker restart/node loss
- consumer: a sensible `basic.qos(prefetch)` balances load; ack after processing (and stay idempotent, since redelivery can duplicate)

This is exactly where RabbitMQ pairs with Outbox to close the dual-write gap.
:::

items.q: How does Kafka guarantee durability: replication, ISR, acks?
items.a:
- each partition has multiple replicas: one leader + followers
- [[b:ISR]] (In-Sync Replicas) = the set of replicas caught up with the leader
- the producer chooses `acks`: `0` (no wait, can lose data), `1` (leader has written), `all/-1` (every ISR has written → most durable)
- `min.insync.replicas` prevents loss when a node is lost

:::deep
[[g:A durable config]]: `acks=all` + `min.insync.replicas=2` + `replication.factor=3` → survives losing 1 broker without data loss; if the ISR drops below the minimum, the producer is rejected (consistency chosen over availability). Enable `enable.idempotence=true` so the producer doesn't create duplicates on retry.

- ordering only holds within a partition → choose a key (`booking_id`) to preserve the event order of a given booking
- [[r:commit the offset *after* processing]] (at-least-once), never auto-commit before processing (risks losing messages on crash)
- a rebalance temporarily pauses consumption → use the cooperative-sticky assignor to reduce the 'stop-the-world' effect
:::

items.q: Ordering: how do the two brokers guarantee it?
items.a:
- [[b:Kafka]]: ordering *within a single partition*. To preserve order for an entity, use that entity as the key (same key → same partition). [[r:There is no global ordering across partitions.]] - [[b:RabbitMQ]]: ordering within a queue with a single consumer; with multiple competing consumers, ordering isn't guaranteed
KafkaRabbitMQ
Ordering unita single partitiona queue with one consumer
How it's assignedmessage key hashed to a partitionrouting key targets exactly one queue
Parallelism while preserving orderyes: multiple partitions, one stream per keyno: adding a consumer breaks order
What breaks orderingchanging partition count, retrying via another topicrequeueing, multiple competing consumers
:::deep - [[r:increasing partition count later]] remaps keys to different partitions → historical order is no longer contiguous (plan partitioning up front) - RabbitMQ: multiple competing consumers or requeueing scrambles order OTA: events for a given `booking_id` (created→paid→issued→cancelled) must land on the same partition so the consumer can build correct state; if global ordering is required (rare) → use 1 partition (losing scale) or reorder on the consumer side with a sequence number. :::

items.q: DLQ and poison messages — how are they handled?
items.a:
A message that keeps failing ([[r:poison]]) blocks the queue if retried forever.

- after N failures → move it to a [[g:Dead-Letter Queue]] so it doesn't clog the main flow → investigate/fix/replay
- retry with exponential backoff + jitter, with a retry limit
- Kafka: retry topic + DLT

:::warn Interview trap
Two follow-up questions usually trip people up. *'Where does the retry live?'* — retrying inline in the consumer blocks the rest of the partition behind it, which is why Kafka needs a separate retry topic. *'How do you safely replay from a DLQ?'* — replay is only safe when the consumer is idempotent (08-message-queue.reliability-delivery-semantics.q6); otherwise every redrive charges the customer again.
:::

:::deep
- pattern: retry with *exponential backoff + jitter* via a retry topic (Kafka) or TTL + dead-letter-exchange (RabbitMQ); after N attempts → DLQ (needs redrive tooling)
- distinguish [[o:transient]] errors (retryable — network) from [[r:permanent]] ones (straight to DLQ — bad schema)
- track DLQ size as an [[g:SLO]] (a growing DLQ signals a systemic bug)

OTA: a 'ticket issuance' message that fails permanently must go to the DLQ and alert an operator (it affects a customer) — [[r:never drop it silently]].
:::

items.q: Idempotent consumer — how do you implement dedup?
items.a:
At-least-once can deliver duplicates → the consumer must detect and skip them:
- a [[b:message id/business key]] + a 'processed' table (unique constraint) written in the *same transaction* as the business effect
- or use operations that are inherently idempotent (UPSERT, setting absolute state)

Kafka also offers an idempotent producer + transactions for 'exactly-once within Kafka's own scope'.

:::tip Bottom line
consumer-side idempotency is a survival requirement for any reliable messaging system — never assume 'each message is processed exactly once'.
:::

:::deep
Two approaches:
- [[g:inherently idempotent operations]] (UPSERT, setting absolute state) — simplest option when it applies
- [[g:dedup table]] with a unique constraint on message-id/business-key, written in the *same transaction* as the business effect ([[r:splitting them leaves a gap where the effect happened but wasn't marked yet]])

OTA: the consumer that 'awards loyalty points' on `payment.succeeded` must be idempotent (the same `payment_id` awards points only once) — a unique `(payment_id)` in a processed table, written in the same tx as the points update.
:::

items.q: The Outbox pattern with a message queue — why is it needed?
items.a:
[[r:Dual write]] (write to the DB, then publish) isn't atomic → the two sides fall out of sync if either one fails. [[g:Outbox]]: write the event into an outbox table in the *same transaction* as the business change; a separate publisher (polling or CDC/Debezium) reads the outbox, publishes, and marks it sent. 
BEGIN;
  UPDATE wallet SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=?;
  INSERT INTO outbox(type,payload,status) VALUES('DEBITED',?,'PENDING');
COMMIT;  -- publisher -> broker -> mark SENT (at-least-once)
Only combining [[g:Publisher Confirms]] (broker received it) with [[g:Outbox]] (DB↔publish atomicity) closes the gap completely. :::deep - dual-write (writing to the DB then publishing to the broker as separate steps) is NOT atomic → a crash between the two steps leaves them inconsistent (the DB says the money moved but the event never went out, or vice versa) - [[g:Outbox]]: write the event into an outbox table in the *same transaction* (DB-local atomicity); a separate publisher (polling, or CDC/Debezium reading the binlog) emits it to the broker and marks it SENT (at-least-once → consumer must be idempotent) OTA: when a booking transitions to PAID, write the state change and a 'PaymentSucceeded' outbox row in one tx → the publisher fans it out to ticketing/notification/loyalty; [[r:never 'write to the DB then call Kafka' directly inside business logic]]. - On the domain side of that same outbox table: what gets published externally is an [[b:integration event]] — a public contract that must be versioned — distinct from an internal domain event (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q3). :::

items.q: Event-driven architecture & event sourcing — concepts and trade-offs?
items.a:
- [[b:Event-driven]]: services communicate via async events → decoupling, scale, resilience
- [[b:Event sourcing]]: the *sequence of events* is the source of truth instead of current state; state = replaying events

**Benefits:** perfect audit trail, time travel, rebuildable views (a great fit for fintech/ledgers).

**Trade-offs:** added complexity, eventual consistency, event versioning, needs [[o:CQRS]] for efficient reads.

:::deep
- [[b:event-driven]] gives decoupling/scale/resilience but makes [[r:reasoning about the overall flow harder]] (logic is scattered across consumers), brings eventual consistency, and needs strong observability (tracing across events)
- [[b:event sourcing]]: state = replay → perfect audit trail, time travel, rebuildable read models; the trade-off is complexity (event versioning/upcasting, snapshots for fast replay, requires CQRS)

OTA: the ledger and a booking's lifecycle are good candidates (every change is an immutable event → easy reconciliation/audit/rebuild); [[r:don't event-source everything]] — event-sourcing simple CRUD is over-engineering.

- Distinguish domain events (internal, free to change) from integration events (public contracts) before committing to event-driven design; conflating the two is the hardest kind of hidden coupling to untangle later (24-domain-driven-design.tactical-modelling-it.q3).
:::
